Hooked

Hooked: how scam texts get you

A text arrives: "Royal Mail: Your package has a £2.99 shipping fee, to pay this now visit [link]. Actions will be taken if you do not pay this fee.". In 2024, Americans reported losing $470 million to scams that started with a text message, five times more than in 2020 (Federal Trade Commission, April 2025).

The text breaks into its parts. Authority, "Royal Mail": 74.5% of 15,503 real scam texts borrowed a trusted name. Distraction, "Your package has a £2.99 shipping fee": 30.7% handed you a problem to fix. Urgency, "to pay this now": 70.4% put you on a clock. The hook, the link: 42% contained one. Threat, "Actions will be taken if you do not pay this fee": 33.7% warned of a penalty.

Then you can look inside a small neural network trained on over 60,000 messages, play a timed scam-or-real game, and check your own messages.

0 of 3 found

  • The web address isn’t Royal Mail’s.
  • A countdown rushes you.
  • It asks for far more than a £2.99 fee needs, like your date of birth.

Pay £2.99, and your card goes with it.

Then another fake message asks for the one-time code your bank sends. That code lets them load your card into Apple Pay or Google Wallet on their own phone, and spend with it.

Source: US Homeland Security Investigations, reported by The Wall Street Journal, October 2025

Day 19. The real pitch.

A fake investment app. Victims are shown fake profits, then asked to put in more, and more.

Who sends them

Mostly machines.

Scam texts usually come from SIM farms: racks of phones and SIM boxes sending automatically, from thousands of numbers at once.

In 2025, the US Secret Service found more than 300 SIM boxes and about 100,000 SIM cards near New York, able to send up to 30 million texts a minute.

So we trained an AI to spot them.

A small neural network, trained on over 60,000 messages, including 14,328 real scam texts. It runs right here on your device.

    What raised the score

    It contains a link. The AI doesn’t check where links lead, so don’t tap it. Go to the company’s official app or website yourself.
